documents.title: The Iterator Is the State Machine

sections.text: I can read a chain of enumerate(), filter(), and take() and understand what it asks for. I find it harder to picture what is actually running. Does each step traverse the data again? What does the chain borrow, and what work stops when we stop asking for values? We'll build a small adapter, extend the pattern to prefix sums, and follow a query over borrowed telemetry records. The aim is to understand how the Iterator contract lets these pieces compose, and how ownership and dispatch affect the code we can write. That also gives us a basis for deciding when an ordinary iterator is enough and when asynchronous streams or coroutines help. C++ ranges provide a useful comparison because they support lazy composition too. Looking at both languages helps distinguish the techniques they share from Rust's compile-time checks on borrowing. This gives us a way to judge the safety and potential costs of an iterator-based design, including which performance claims still need measurement. How Rust iterators work Composing iterators with adapters Prefix sums Ask for two matches Does the order matter? Keep the records where they are A borrowed telemetry query Keep a result while asking for another Static and dynamic dispatch Compiler optimization Asynchronous iteration and coroutines Iterator composition in C++ Choosing the mechanism References I'll assume you can follow a for loop and have met map or filter in some language. You don't need to know Rust's trait system yet. The examples use Rust 2021 or later.

sections.heading: How Rust iterators work
sections.text: Here are four values, printed with their positions: enumerate() adds a position to each value. fn main() { for (index, value) in [1, 2, 3, 4] .into_iter() .enumerate() { println!("{index}: {value}"); } } The output starts at 0: 1 and ends at 3: 4. Somewhere, something remembers which value comes next and which index to attach to it. Rust's iteration protocol puts that responsibility in the iterator. Its required interface is small: The required part of Iterator, with its provided methods omitted. pub trait Iterator { type Item; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>; } A trait describes behavior a type can provide. Here, Item names the type of value it produces. next() asks for one value and returns either Some(value) or None. The &mut self parameter lets the iterator change its own state while answering. A for loop first asks IntoIterator to turn its input into an iterator, then repeatedly asks for the next value. For this simple array, we can sketch the loop like this: A sketch of the iteration behavior, not the complete language desugaring. let values = [10, 20, 30]; let mut iterator = IntoIterator::into_iter(values); while let Some(value) = iterator.next() { println!("{value}"); } The loop stops at the first None. It doesn't need to know whether advancing means moving through an array, following a list, or reading from a file. The Iterator contract allows an implementation to return Some again after returning None. A for loop still stops at that first None. If you need later calls to keep returning None, fuse() supplies that behavior. Iterators implementing FusedIterator already promise it. This becomes relevant when we reach asynchronous streams: None is not a general-purpose instruction to wait and try again later.

sections.heading: Composing iterators with adapters
sections.text: An adapter wraps an iterator and implements Iterator itself. That shared interface lets us connect adapters: each one can use another as its source, without knowing how that source obtains its values. To add a position, our wrapper needs to hold the source iterator and a counter: A small numbering adapter. The counter starts at zero when we construct it. struct Indexed<I> { source: I, index: usize, } impl<I: Iterator> Iterator for Indexed<I> { type Item = (usize, I::Item); fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { let value = self.source.next()?; let index = self.index; self.index += 1; Some((index, value)) } } State between calls. The wrapper owns its source iterator and a counter. The source may itself borrow a collection; storing it here preserves that relationship. The same contract on both sides. I must implement Iterator, and Indexed<I> implements it too. Another adapter can use this wrapper as its source. Ask the source for one item. ? returns None if the source has no item on this call. The counter advances only after an item is obtained. I stands for whichever iterator we wrap. The bound I: Iterator lets us call its next() method, and I::Item names the type it produces. Our adapter returns a pair: a position and that source item. Because Indexed<I> also implements Iterator, it gets the trait's provided methods, including filter() and take(). The ? after self.source.next() returns None immediately if the source returned None. Otherwise, it extracts the value. We save the current index, increment the counter for next time, and return the pair. We can construct one with the counter set to zero and step through it ourselves: Each call advances the source and the counter held by the same object. let mut indexed = Indexed { source: [10, 20].into_iter(), index: 0, }; assert_eq!(indexed.next(), Some((0, 10))); assert_eq!(indexed.next(), Some((1, 20))); assert_eq!(indexed.next(), None); The state persists in these fields between calls to next(). The method returns each time; the next call uses the values left by the previous one. Rust's standard-library Enumerate stores the same two pieces of state. It also implements shortcuts for operations such as nth(), fold(), and try_fold(). We will come back to why those matter. The example uses usize, just as Enumerate does. Its index can overflow on a sufficiently long sequence. The public enumerate() documentation says that enumeration can panic or produce an incorrect count when the counter overflows, with a panic guaranteed when overflow checks are enabled. This adapter is a model of ordinary enumeration, not an arbitrary-precision counter.

sections.heading: Prefix sums
sections.text: The same structure can produce prefix sums. Keep a running total alongside the source, add each incoming value, and yield the new total. For 3, 1, 4, 2, the prefix sums are 3, 4, 8, 10. A custom prefix-sum adapter composes with the standard enumerate() and take() adapters. struct PrefixSums<I> { source: I, total: u64, } impl<I: Iterator<Item = u64>> Iterator for PrefixSums<I> { type Item = u64; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> { self.total += self.source.next()?; Some(self.total) } } let sums: Vec<_> = PrefixSums { source: [3u64, 1, 4, 2].into_iter(), total: 0, } .enumerate() .take(3) .collect(); assert_eq!(sums, vec![(0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 8)]); Update the retained total. Each successful pull adds one source value. The same field holds 3, then 4, then 8 as the caller advances. Let the consumer stop the work. take(3) stops before asking for a fourth sum. The final input, 2, is not read by this chain. This time the bound is narrower: the source must produce u64 values so we can add them to the total. The adapters after it still work through Iterator. enumerate() numbers the sums, and take(3) stops the chain before the last input is read. Neither needs to know how PrefixSums maintains its total. As with the index counter, a reusable numeric adapter needs a policy for overflow. These small sums fit in u64. The standard library also provides scan(), which can express the same running total using stored state and a closure.

sections.heading: Ask for two matches
sections.text: Now suppose we want the first two even values and their positions in the original input: Two results retain their original positions; inspect() counts three source values. let values = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]; let mut examined = 0; let result: Vec<_> = values .into_iter() .inspect(|_| examined += 1) .enumerate() .filter(|(_, value)| value % 2 == 0) .take(2) .collect(); assert_eq!(examined, 3); assert_eq!(result, vec![(0, 10), (2, 12)]); enumerate() produces pairs. filter() keeps pairs whose value is even. Its predicate borrows each item as &Self::Item to test it; an accepted item is then passed on by value. With borrowed source items, that test adds another layer of references. take(2) allows at most two items through, and collect() gathers them into a vector. It is easy to imagine a separate pass at every dot: number all five values, put the even ones somewhere, then copy the first two. These adapters can instead pass requests and values through the chain without building those intermediate collections. Think of asking the outer iterator for a match. It asks its source, which eventually reaches the array. The value 10 comes back with index 0, passes the filter, and becomes the first result. The second request takes more work. 11 gets index 1 but fails the filter. The filter asks again, receives (2, 12), and accepts it. Once take(2) has supplied two results, it stops asking the source for more. Figure 1: Requests travel toward the source; accepted items return to the consumer. The second output needs two source reads. This is a semantic trace, not a literal optimized call graph. Open the full-size diagram The last two values aren't pulled through inspect(). Constructing the adapter chain didn't scan the input; consuming it caused the work. The final vector has storage of its own, but there is no vector between each adapter. There is a limit to this control. Asking for one output can require examining many inputs. A filter over an infinite sequence with no matches never returns a match. Calling take(2) limits the number of outputs; it does not promise two source reads, a time limit, or a bounded amount of work.

sections.heading: Does the order matter?
sections.text: Move enumerate() after the filter: Filtering first numbers the surviving values, not their original positions. let values = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]; let result: Vec<_> = values .into_iter() .filter(|value| value % 2 == 0) .enumerate() .take(2) .collect(); assert_eq!(result, vec![(0, 10), (1, 12)]); Now 12 has index 1. Only the surviving values reach the counter. In a diagnostic tool, that could turn an original record position into a match number. Both are useful, but we need to choose which one we mean.

sections.heading: Keep the records where they are
sections.text: Numbering works the same way whether the source produces owned values or references. The difference travels through Item: Expression Item type What the loop receives names.iter() &String A shared reference to each string names.iter_mut() &mut String An exclusive reference to each string names.into_iter() String Ownership of each string from this vector Here are all three with the same adapter: The first two loops borrow the vector; the last consumes it. let mut names = vec![ String::from("Alice"), String::from("Bob"), ]; // Borrow the elements. for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { println!("{i}: {name}"); } // Mutably borrow the elements. for (_, name) in names.iter_mut().enumerate() { name.push('!'); } // Transfer ownership of the elements. for (i, name) in names.into_iter().enumerate() { println!("{i}: {name}"); } The last loop moves the strings out of the vector. It doesn't clone their contents, and we cannot use names afterward as though it still owned them. In the earlier loops, Rust checks that uses of the references respect their lifetimes and exclusive access requirements. enumerate() doesn't need separate code for each case. Its pair contains I::Item, whatever that happens to be. It adds a counter while leaving the ownership relationship intact. Ownership also determines cleanup. When we drop an adapter, its owned fields are dropped too, including the source iterator and any closure state. If a chain consumes a vector with into_iter(), dropping it also drops the vector iterator's unconsumed elements. A chain built with iter() only borrows the vector; dropping that chain leaves the elements in place. Early termination stops further pulls, but cleanup can still do work.

sections.heading: A borrowed telemetry query
sections.text: Consider readings already loaded into a buffer. We want unverified readings above a latency threshold, with their original positions. We can offer that search without copying matching records into another collection: Returning a borrowed iterator lets the caller choose how many matches to inspect. #[derive(Debug)] struct Reading { device_id: u64, latency_ms: u32, verified: bool, } fn suspicious<'a>( readings: &'a [Reading], threshold_ms: u32, ) -> impl Iterator<Item = (usize, &'a Reading)> + 'a { readings .iter() .enumerate() .filter(move |(_, reading)| { reading.latency_ms > threshold_ms && !reading.verified }) } Borrow from the caller's buffer. The yielded &'a Reading points into readings. Returning this iterator does not copy the records or extend the input's lifetime. Keep the threshold with the predicate. move captures threshold_ms by value. Since u32 is Copy, the closure keeps a copy; the source iterator still borrows the readings. Use this main() with Reading and suspicious() above. fn main() { let readings = [ Reading { device_id: 101, latency_ms: 150, verified: true, }, Reading { device_id: 102, latency_ms: 400, verified: false, }, Reading { device_id: 103, latency_ms: 350, verified: false, }, ]; for (index, reading) in suspicious(&readings, 250).take(2) { println!("{index}: {reading:?}"); } } Choose how many matches to inspect. The first reading is verified and excluded. This call prints the entries at positions 1 and 2 without collecting them into a new vector. The function describes how to find a reading. Its caller can ask for two, find the first, or count every match. Returning an iterator keeps that choice open. The lifetime label 'a ties the references in the results to the borrowed input. It doesn't extend the life of the buffer or copy it somewhere safe. If a caller tries to keep using the search after the readings have gone away, the program fails to compile. The move keyword makes the closure capture threshold_ms by value. Because u32 implements Copy, the closure stores a copy of the threshold instead of borrowing the function's local variable. The readings remain borrowed through the source iterator.

sections.heading: Keep a result while asking for another
sections.text: Using the same readings, we can retain two matches and drop the search before using them: Returned references remain usable after the iterator is dropped, while the readings stay valid. let mut matches = suspicious(&readings, 250); let first = matches.next().expect("first matching reading"); let second = matches.next().expect("second matching reading"); drop(matches); println!("{first:?}"); println!("{second:?}"); Keep a result while advancing. first borrows a reading in the input buffer. It does not retain the temporary mutable borrow used to advance matches, so the next call is allowed. Drop the search, keep the references. The iterator owns its adapter state, but only borrows the readings. Destroying that state does not destroy the caller's buffer. Each call briefly borrows the iterator mutably so it can advance. The returned references borrow readings, not the iterator object. Holding the first result doesn't keep that call's mutable borrow of the iterator open, so we can ask for another. Dropping the iterator leaves both references usable as long as the underlying readings remain valid. The signature separates these lifetimes. Item is fixed for the iterator type; it isn't parameterized by the temporary borrow of each next() call. In this search it contains &'a Reading, with 'a tied to the input slice. A mutable iterator must also make it safe to retain several results, for example by yielding references to distinct elements. That is a limit on what ordinary Iterator can express. It cannot generally lend out a reference into its own scratch buffer and then overwrite that buffer on the next call while the reference is still in use. Such an API needs a different ownership arrangement, or a lending-style contract that ties each result to the call's borrow. We don't need that here: the caller already owns the buffer. impl Iterator hides a concrete return type that would be awkward to write out. The compiler still knows that type, including the closure and the wrapped iterators. Returning it this way does not introduce a boxed object or a virtual method call.

sections.heading: Static and dynamic dispatch
sections.text: The trait tells us what an iterator can do. Rust lets us choose how a call reaches the implementation. Here are two functions asking for the same thing: A concrete generic parameter. fn next_static<I: Iterator<Item = u64>>( source: &mut I, ) -> Option<u64> { source.next() } A borrowed trait object. fn next_dynamic( source: &mut dyn Iterator<Item = u64>, ) -> Option<u64> { source.next() } With next_static, the compiler knows the concrete I and can specialize the function for it. This is static dispatch. With next_dynamic, the function accepts a trait object. Its reference carries a pointer to the iterator state and vtable metadata used to find the method at runtime. This is dynamic dispatch. The iterator still holds its state in either case. Dispatch changes how we reach the method, not who drives the sequence or whether it is lazy. Notice that next_dynamic borrows an iterator. It doesn't allocate one. We can pass a reference to an iterator already stored in a local variable. Heap allocation and dynamic dispatch are separate choices. For our telemetry query, each adapter and closure has a concrete type. suspicious() returns the resulting chain through impl Iterator, which hides its name without erasing that type. The compiler keeps the information needed to specialize calls and consider inlining them. We haven't needed a runtime choice of implementation between stages. A concrete wrapper can still contain a dynamically dispatched iterator. Adding take() around a trait object doesn't make calls to that underlying source static. Suppose a query can return every value or only even ones, depending on a setting read at runtime: Two concrete iterator types share one boxed return type, while the input remains borrowed. fn choose_values<'a>( values: &'a [u64], only_even: bool, ) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = u64> + 'a> { if only_even { Box::new(values.iter().copied().filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)) } else { Box::new(values.iter().copied()) } } The branches construct different types: one includes a filter and the other doesn't. Box<dyn Iterator<Item = u64> + 'a> gives them a common return type. The box owns the iterator state; the slice remains borrowed. The lifetime bound keeps that borrow valid, and Item = u64 tells callers what either implementation produces. A plain impl Iterator return cannot hide a different concrete type in each branch. For this particular condition we could instead use one filter with a configurable predicate. An enum could also represent a fixed set of alternatives. A trait object becomes useful when we want a common interface without making that set part of its type. Here the box supplies owned heap storage for the iterator, not a newly allocated record on every call. The earlier &mut dyn Iterator example supplies dynamic dispatch without that storage choice. Both retain the usual ownership and borrowing checks. Static specialization can increase generated code size and compilation work when many concrete types use the same generic code. Dynamic dispatch can let a consumer share one implementation across those types. An indirect call may make inlining harder, although the optimizer can sometimes recover the target. If this trade-off matters to the application, it needs measurement., Traits must satisfy Rust's dyn compatibility rules to support trait objects. Iterator does, once we specify its associated Item type. Its next() method can be called through the vtable. Many generic adapter and consumer methods instead require Self: Sized, which excludes those methods from the dynamically callable interface. That doesn't prevent further composition. A sized wrapper such as Box<dyn Iterator<Item = u64>> or &mut dyn Iterator<Item = u64> itself implements Iterator. We can add adapters around it. The outer adapter has a concrete type, while requests reaching the erased source still use its dynamic interface. A generic wrapper doesn't automatically make every call inside it static. For a visual tour of trait-object pointers, see Sofía Belén López Vicens's Visualizing Rust's VTables: How dyn Trait Works in Memory. Exact byte layouts and vtable slot offsets should not be treated as a stable Rust ABI.

sections.heading: Compiler optimization
sections.text: An iterator chain can compile to code similar to a hand-written loop. Rust specializes generic code for concrete types through monomorphization. Inlining can then bring operations from different adapters together so the optimizer can work across them. For example, these functions calculate the same sum. The wrapping operations make overflow behavior explicit: A loop that squares even values and adds them with wrapping arithmetic. pub fn manual(input: &[u64]) -> u64 { let mut sum = 0u64; for &x in input { if x % 2 == 0 { sum = sum.wrapping_add(x.wrapping_mul(x)); } } sum } The same calculation expressed as an iterator chain. pub fn adapted(input: &[u64]) -> u64 { input .iter() .copied() .filter(|x| x % 2 == 0) .map(|x| x.wrapping_mul(x)) .fold(0u64, |sum, x| sum.wrapping_add(x)) } Inlining and loop optimization can make the generated code resemble the handwritten version. Whether they do so for a particular program depends on the compiler, target, optimization settings, and surrounding code. We would have to inspect that output and benchmark representative inputs to make a performance claim. There is another wrinkle in our request-by-request picture. The standard library can implement a consumer such as fold() by passing the whole accumulation through the adapters. Its Enumerate implementation has specialized fold() and try_fold() methods, so consuming a chain need not literally become a tower of next() calls. The pull model explains the sequence's behavior; optimized bulk operations can implement it differently. Some costs are visible without a benchmark. Our simple adapter chain doesn't require an intermediate collection at every step. It uses concrete types instead of a required virtual call at every boundary. Neither fact makes the predicate free, guarantees vectorization, or eliminates allocation in user-supplied code. In Fast Writes, Fresh Reads, moving work into a background thread introduced replay and coordination costs. Here, calling filter() doesn't start a worker at all. The caller runs the predicate as it consumes the iterator. A fluent chain of methods doesn't, by itself, tell us where computation runs.

sections.heading: Asynchronous iteration and coroutines
sections.text: The telemetry example starts with a slice already in memory. A live connection has another possibility: there is no new reading yet, but more may arrive. An ordinary iterator can block inside next() until data arrives. Its interface doesn't say whether a call will return quickly. What it lacks is a way to return "not ready" together with an asynchronous wakeup arrangement. The Stream trait from futures-core adds that distinction: The poll_next signature from futures-core::Stream, with surrounding declarations omitted. fn poll_next( self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>>; Result Meaning Ready(Some(value)) A value is available Ready(None) The stream has ended Pending No value yet; arrange a wakeup when progress may be possible Context gives the implementation access to a waker. Pin supports implementations whose state must stay at a stable location while pinned. Those requirements serve asynchronous execution, beyond the in-memory loop we started with. Rust's async computations use the Future protocol. The compiler represents their progress in a generated state machine, retaining what is needed across an await., A coroutine lets a function suspend and later resume from where it stopped. A synchronous generator uses that ability to yield values one at a time, with its consumer requesting each resumption. When producing a value involves nested loops and several yield points, that can be easier to follow than a hand-written state machine. Our numbering adapter needed only a source and a counter; more complicated control flow can justify the extra mechanism. There is also a boundary between local demand and system backpressure. A caller can stop pulling this iterator while a device, broker, or network buffer keeps receiving data. The capacity, loss, and admission policies from Backpressure in a Telemetry Pipeline still need to exist outside the iterator. A take() at the end of a chain doesn't bound every queue upstream.

sections.heading: Iterator composition in C++
sections.text: C++ ranges let us build a similar lazy pipeline, so they give us a way to ask which parts of the design are specific to Rust. C++23 provides enumeration directly: C++23's standard enumeration view needs no custom coroutine generator. #include <array> #include <iostream> #include <ranges> int main() { std::array values{1, 2, 3, 4}; for (auto [index, value] : std::views::enumerate(values)) { std::cout << index << ": " << value << '\n'; } } C++20 ranges already offered lazy composition; C++23 added this standard numbering adapter. Comparing a small Rust enumerate() call with the plumbing of a hand-built C++ coroutine generator would measure two different implementation choices. C++ ranges use iterator and sentinel interfaces, concepts, and views. A sentinel marks the end condition; it need not have the same type as the iterator. Those interfaces support lazy computation and compiler optimization too. Rust doesn't have exclusive access to that technique. Both languages support references, moves, and deterministic destruction. Rust's borrowing rules add compiler checks for reference lifetimes and exclusive access across the composition. C++ APIs can express ownership and borrowing relationships, but ordinary references don't generally carry the same static checks. The borrowing example is where I find the comparison most useful: who must establish that these records are still valid when a result is used?

sections.heading: Choosing the mechanism
sections.text: We can now account for the numbered loop. The source remembers its position. Enumerate remembers a counter. A filter may ask several times before passing a value along. The consumer decides whether to keep asking, and the item type preserves whether the result owns or borrows its data. For a query over an existing buffer, returning a borrowed iterator lets the caller inspect a few matches without first building a collection. If obtaining the next value requires waiting for a socket, an ordinary iterator can block inside next(). When the caller must yield execution while waiting and resume when progress becomes possible, the interface needs an asynchronous readiness and wakeup protocol. If later work needs to revisit or sort the results, collecting them may be the right choice. When I read an iterator chain now, I try to picture the state each adapter holds and the work one request can trigger. That gives me a way to judge the abstraction before making assumptions about its speed.

A client submits a device event. The service replies accepted. An operator refreshes the dashboard and still sees the old value. The event may already be safely recorded. The table behind the dashboard is still catching up. Without some indication of its progress, the operator has no way to tell a delayed view from a missing update. Decide what “accepted” means Choose who pays for the lookup Pay when somebody reads Pay before replying Pay after replying Put freshness in the answer Give unfinished work a budget Decide who owns the batch What changes at the handoff Look at the allocation pattern Ask whether the same work is necessary Change which bytes move Spend memory and maintenance where they help Schedule maintenance with foreground demand Measure acknowledgement and visibility What the local runs showed Choose the language at the constraint that matters References Recording an event and making it available to readers can finish at different times. The service needs to say which of those it has promised when it replies. Updating the table before replying closes this visibility gap for readers of that table. Moving the update into a worker can shorten the acknowledgement path, provided the service tracks the work still waiting. If lookups are rare, it may be cheaper to scan the journal when a query arrives and maintain no table at all. I want to compare those choices through a small journal design in Go and Rust. The interesting question is where the lookup work belongs, and what a fast acknowledgement leaves the service to finish afterward. The code also gives us a concrete place to compare the languages' ownership and synchronization rules. sections.heading: Decide what “accepted” means
sections.text: Consider a service that records unconditional device updates. Ingestion is its main job. Latest-value lookups happen less often and can tolerate some delay, as long as the service reports it. The lookup table is a projection: a representation derived from the journal to serve those reads. For this design, accepting a write means appending its records to a local journal and successfully synchronizing the file. Only then may the background worker consume them. The reply confirms that the journal has recorded the write; the projection may still be behind. The writer publishes its progress after synchronization: append bytes → synchronize file → publish completed position These excerpts show that ordering for synchronized writes with a background projection. They omit setup and instrumentation. The Rust writer here is a file; a user-space buffering wrapper would have to be flushed before synchronizing the underlying file., Publishing after synchronization: Go, with explicit error propagation. if err = writeAll(f, buffer[:count*width]); err != nil { return } if err = f.Sync(); err != nil { return } p.mu.Lock() p.head = base + count p.cv.Broadcast() p.mu.Unlock() Publishing after synchronization: Rust, with error propagation through ?. writer.write_all(&buffer[..count * WIDTH])?; writer.sync_all()?; { let mut state = p.mu.lock() .expect("projection lock poisoned"); state.head = base + count; p.cv.notify_all(); } Neither version advances head if synchronization reports an error. The mutex makes the new position visible to the worker; file synchronization handles a separate obligation to storage., , Rust's write_all keeps writing until the buffer is consumed or it encounters an error it cannot retry. The companion's Go helper loops over partial progress and rejects zero progress. Neither operation makes a batch atomic: an error can leave part of it in the file. Both programs stop on a write or synchronization error instead of retrying an uncertain append., Creating the journal is part of the persistence protocol too. Both programs create a new file exclusively and, in synchronized mode, synchronize the empty file and its containing directory before timing writes. On Linux, file synchronization alone does not necessarily persist the directory entry. These setup steps still do not qualify the programs for every power-loss scenario. A crash after synchronization but before the reply can also leave a recorded write that the client believes failed. Retrying safely requires a request identity or an application rule for duplicate updates. Delaying the projection does not resolve this acknowledgement ambiguity. The lookup projection is optional for accepting these unconditional updates. If acceptance depends on a uniqueness check or a conditional update, the service needs sufficiently current state to make that decision before accepting the write.

sections.heading: Pay when somebody reads
sections.text: With no lookup table, a query can scan backward in blocks from a captured journal boundary. It stops at the first record for the device. A recent value may be quick to find; a device with no record requires scanning the entire captured history. This avoids maintaining a table for events nobody queries. It becomes expensive when an investigation asks for many old values or missing devices. Infrequent reads can still have a response-time requirement.

sections.heading: Pay before replying
sections.text: The eager writer updates the in-memory table after synchronization and before replying. A subsequent reader of that same table, using the same lock, can see the write or a later update. A different replica or response cache needs its own visibility guarantee. The table can remain in memory because the journal is enough to rebuild it. Persisting the table would be a separate choice to reduce recovery time. For a small table, updating it directly may cost less than coordinating a worker.

sections.heading: Pay after replying
sections.text: A background worker replays the published journal prefix into the table. The writer can usually reply without waiting for that replay. The service does, however, pay for another read pass, decoding and checksum verification, as well as worker coordination. Those reads may hit the page cache and avoid physical I/O, but still use CPU and memory bandwidth. Moving replay out of the acknowledgement path can shorten the response while increasing total work. For a service with rare lookups, a scan may be enough. Frequent reads can justify a table. A worker is worth adding when the shorter acknowledgement path is useful enough to pay for replay and delayed visibility.

sections.heading: Put freshness in the answer
sections.text: Suppose the journal is published through record 10,000 and the projection has applied through 9,700. The view is missing 300 events. These are illustrative positions, not benchmark results. Figure 2: The view covers a journal prefix; a device's last-update position may be older. Positions and widths are illustrative. A live freshness-wait API is not implemented by the benchmark. Open the full-size diagram A value alone hides that gap. A value accompanied by as_of_sequence = 9,700 states the view's boundary. The value's own last-update sequence may be older; a particular device need not change in every batch. The view must represent a contiguous prefix: 0 <= indexed <= head projection = apply every record from 1 through indexed, in order A single worker reads and validates the next batch outside the lock. It then applies the table changes and advances its position in the same critical section. Readers must never observe the new position with the old table. Updating data and progress together: Go fields protected by convention. p.mu.Lock() for _, r := range decoded[:count] { p.entries[r.Key] = Entry{r.Seq, r.Value} } p.indexed = start + count p.cv.Broadcast() p.mu.Unlock() Updating data and progress together: Rust state accessed through a guard. { let mut state = self.mu.lock() .expect("projection lock poisoned"); for r in &decoded[..count] { state.entries[r.key as usize] = Entry { seq: r.seq, value: r.value, }; } state.indexed = start + count; self.cv.notify_all(); } A live reader must copy the entry and the projection position under that same lock. For read-your-writes, the write response can return its journal sequence. A reader waits for indexed > required_sequence= and copies the result while still holding the lock. It may see a later update to the same device: the position is a minimum freshness requirement, not an exact historical snapshot. A timeout says the view did not reach that position before the deadline. The recorded write may still be waiting to appear. Here, “latest” means last in journal order. A delayed device observation appended later will replace an earlier entry, even if its measurement timestamp is older. A service that needs the newest measurement instead needs an event-time or version comparison and a rule for ties. Go places a mutex beside the protected fields. The compiler does not require callers to acquire it. Package boundaries, review, and race-enabled tests help enforce the convention; a race detector only observes executed paths. Rust's Mutex supplies protected access through a guard, whose scope makes the lock lifetime visible. Arc lets threads share ownership; the projection still needs synchronization for its mutable state., Rust will still compile code that advances indexed too early while holding the correct lock. Preserving the contiguous prefix is our responsibility in either language. Reading and decoding outside the lock also matters because the critical section blocks readers and the writer's progress publication. Parallel replay workers would need an ordered commit protocol: a later batch finishing first must not advance the position past an unfinished earlier batch. The live freshness API also needs its own tests; queries made only after catch-up cannot exercise it.

sections.heading: Give unfinished work a budget
sections.text: A worker can finish a short test after traffic stops and still be too slow for the service's normal arrival rate. Assumed input rate Assumed worker rate Backlog added in 10 seconds 300,000 records/s 270,000 records/s 300,000 records Illustration, not measurement: 30,000 additional records per second × 10 seconds. At 32 bytes per record, the outstanding journal suffix is 9.6 MB. A larger queue gives the worker longer to absorb a burst. If that rate difference persists, the dashboard falls further behind and shutdown has more work to drain. The writer can limit that lag by checking capacity before appending another batch: current lag + next batch <= lag limit head - indexed + count <= limit When the condition fails, the writer waits. Once the budget fills, a sustained write rate is constrained by the worker's progress. Measuring only the earlier fast acknowledgements would hide that limit. Figure 3: A record budget makes the writer wait for replay instead of admitting an ever-growing gap. These trajectories are schematic. The bound is on record count, not age, journal size or upstream queues. Open the full-size diagram Waiting for capacity: Go's condition variable has a locker. func (p *projection) reserve(count, limit int) error { p.mu.Lock() defer p.mu.Unlock() for p.head-p.indexed+count > limit && p.failure == nil { p.cv.Wait() } return p.failure } Waiting for capacity: Rust's wait consumes and returns the guard. fn reserve(&self, count: usize, limit: usize) -> io::Result<()> { let mut state = self.mu.lock() .expect("projection lock poisoned"); while state.head - state.indexed + count > limit && state.failure.is_none() { state = self.cv.wait(state) .expect("projection lock poisoned"); } match &state.failure { Some(error) => Err(invalid(error.clone())), None => Ok(()), } } Both waits release the mutex and reacquire it before continuing. Both loops must recheck the predicate. Go's wait requires notification to return, but notification does not imply the predicate is true. Rust additionally permits spurious wakeups., The full worker code records I/O or decoding failures under the lock and notifies waiters. Neither wait has a request deadline or cancellation path, though. Storage that stalls without returning an error can leave callers waiting indefinitely. The full programs reject a lag limit smaller than the configured batch size and cap record counts and batch sizes for their 64-bit target. Those checks matter if this excerpt is reused: an oversized batch can never fit, and unbounded position arithmetic can overflow., These excerpts assume one writer. Despite its name, the method checks capacity without reserving it. Two writers could both pass the check and then exceed the limit. Multiple writers need reservations or serialized admission, whichever language implements them. The limit bounds how many accepted records are waiting for replay, not how long they have waited. Even one event can remain stale indefinitely if the worker stops. It also leaves other budgets untouched: the full journal can keep growing and requests may queue upstream. Variable-size or variable-cost events may need a byte or work budget instead of a record count.

sections.heading: Decide who owns the batch
sections.text: In the replay design, the worker owns a read descriptor and reusable buffers. The writer publishes a position and has no batch memory to share with it. This keeps ownership simple, at the cost of replay and decoding. An alternative sends the decoded batch directly after persistence. This avoids replay, but the writer must not reuse the batch while the worker is still reading it. The next two functions show different handoff contracts. Go keeps the caller's original buffer; Rust transfers it. These are teaching examples from examples/handoff, separate from the journal policies being compared. Go: keep the original and copy the records for the worker. func EnqueueCopy( ctx context.Context, out chan<- []Record, batch []Record, ) error { owned := append([]Record(nil), batch...) select { case out <- owned: return nil case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err() } } Rust: move the existing allocation to the worker. pub fn enqueue_owned( out: &SyncSender<Vec<Record>>, batch: Vec<Record>, ) -> Result<(), SendError<Vec<Record>>> { out.send(batch) }

sections.heading: What changes at the handoff
sections.text: A Go channel transfers the slice descriptor, not an independent backing array. Sending it does not prohibit later access by the sender, nor establish that processing is finished. This version copies the batch to preserve the caller's ability to reuse the original after the call., Rust moves the vector into the channel. The caller cannot keep using the moved value, and the backing array is not cloned. If the receiver disconnects before the send succeeds, SendError carries the unsent vector back., , Figure 4: These teaching functions have different caller contracts: Go retains an original and sends a copy; Rust transfers the existing allocation. Both need a return protocol to reuse storage. Sending is not processing completion. Open the full-size diagram Successful submission still does not mean the worker has applied the batch. A buffered send can finish before the receiver takes it; even an unbuffered handoff only confirms receipt. The projection's progress position remains the way to tell whether processing has finished., Choice Go Rust Transfer without copying payload Possible; sender relinquishes access by convention Ownership move restricts subsequent use Retain an independently mutable original Copy the records Clone or otherwise copy the records Reuse storage after worker completion Return buffer through an agreed protocol Return the owned vector through a protocol Waiting in the shown API Context can cancel the wait Standard send waits for capacity or disconnection Moving a reusable buffer transfers its allocation too: let submitted = std::mem::take(&mut batch); enqueue_owned(&tx, submitted)?; // `batch` is now empty; its former allocation moved to the worker. The writer therefore needs replacement storage for its next batch. A pool with a return path can reuse allocations in either language. Go relies on a convention that the sender stops accessing transferred storage; Rust checks the move at compile time. These records contain only integers, so the Go slice copy duplicates all record data. With pointers or nested slices it would be shallow. The caller must keep the input stable while copying, and channel closure must be coordinated with sends. The Go function copies before it checks cancellation. If both the send and cancellation are ready, the select may choose either, so cancellation has no priority. Rust's standard SyncSender::send takes no cancellation token at all; a deadline-aware submission protocol needs additional machinery or another channel API., A bounded channel limits queued messages, but callers can still allocate batches before blocking on it. In this Go example, each waiting caller retains an extra copy. Bound the number of producers and batch sizes, or acquire capacity before allocating, if the channel is meant to enforce a memory budget. The same issue applies to Rust producers retaining owned vectors while waiting to send. Direct handoff would still need journal-based recovery after a crash. A batch leaving memory must not become a hole in the projection merely because no worker had consumed it yet.

sections.heading: Look at the allocation pattern
sections.text: Both table examples use a dense array indexed by bounded integer device IDs. Each entry holds two 64-bit integers. Updating an entry replaces those values without requiring a separate allocation for the update. Go's table: one slice of values. type Entry struct { Seq uint64 Value uint64 } entries := make([]Entry, keyCount) Rust's table: one vector of values. #[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)] struct Entry { seq: u64, value: u64, } let entries = vec![Entry::default(); key_count]; Each logical entry contributes 16 bytes of field data. That excludes collection metadata and allocator overhead; actual memory use needs measuring on the target. Dense IDs make the layout reasonable. Sparse IDs could waste most of the table, while a hash table would introduce its own storage and hashing costs. In Go, keeping pointers out of this table reduces the collector's scanning work relative to a pointer-rich graph. To judge the remaining cost, inspect allocation rate and retained heap as well as collector CPU, including allocation assists. Pause time tells only part of that story. Rust has no tracing garbage collector in these examples. Destruction and deallocation still take time: dropping an owned structure or the last strong Arc can run cleanup on a latency-sensitive thread. The work depends on what is owned; a vector of these integer-only entries has much less to destroy than a graph of objects with custom cleanup., These examples avoid a long-lived graph of per-event objects. Their allocation pattern says little about a service with string keys or variable payloads.

sections.heading: Ask whether the same work is necessary
sections.text: Moving work to a different thread is only one way to change the trade-off. Storage research also changes the representation, memory allocation, and amount of maintenance required. The RUM conjecture describes a trade-off between read cost, update cost, and memory or storage overhead: optimizing two tends to come at the expense of the third. It is a conjecture about access methods, not a rule that fixes the best design for this service. For our projection, it is a reason to include space in the comparison alongside read and write costs. Freshness and backlog are additional service constraints.

sections.heading: Change which bytes move
sections.text: WiscKey (FAST 2016) keeps keys and value locations in an LSM-tree while storing values in a separate log. This reduces value movement during compaction, at the cost of managing that log and changing range-query access patterns. It suggests a useful question for our worker: how much of each event actually needs to be copied, decoded, or reorganized?

sections.heading: Spend memory and maintenance where they help
sections.text: Monkey (SIGMOD 2017) distributes Bloom-filter memory across LSM levels to reduce the combined false-positive cost of lookups. Giving every level the same bits per key misses that opportunity. Dostoevsky (SIGMOD 2018) reduces merging where it contributes little to point lookups, long range queries, or space reclamation. Its design also accounts for the different needs of short range queries. That distinction matters when deciding which maintenance work earns its cost. For the journal, the corresponding question is which representation earns its maintenance cost under the queries people actually make.

sections.heading: Schedule maintenance with foreground demand
sections.text: EcoTune (SIGMOD 2025) treats compaction as an investment of CPU and I/O resources to improve future queries. HATS (FAST 2026), implemented in Cassandra, combines replica selection for reads with adaptive compaction rate control., Neither paper implements this projection protocol. They address a problem the worker shares with compaction: background tasks compete with foreground requests for the resources intended to make those requests faster. A writer can slow down even when it never waits directly for the worker. Both still use the same CPU, caches, memory bandwidth, and storage device. For the journal, this leaves several choices worth measuring: reduce the bytes replayed, maintain less state, or schedule replay around foreground demand. Changing threads is only one option.

sections.heading: Measure acknowledgement and visibility
sections.text: The producer needs an acknowledgement. The operator needs a sufficiently fresh answer. The service must sustain both without accumulating an ever-growing backlog. Whose requirement? Measure What a misleading result leaves out Producer Arrival-to-acknowledgement latency Upstream queueing and batch formation Operator Visibility delay and lookup latency at a stated freshness Whether the answer includes the write Service Lag, catch-up time, CPU, memory, and physical I/O Work still unfinished when the timer stops Recovery Time to the required serving state Which representations must actually be rebuilt The companion records batch acknowledgement timing, time in the lag gate, maximum record lag, and catch-up time after writes stop. Its lookups run over the same completed history in all three designs. The gate timer includes acquiring and checking the mutex even when no wait is needed, so it is not a pure blocked-time measure. Those post-drain lookups still leave the operator's experience untested. To measure live freshness and interference, queries must run while writes continue. A timer around a ready batch also excludes upstream queueing and time spent waiting for the batch to fill. The companion uses the same 32-byte record format, deterministic input, batching, table layout, worker batch size, and lag limit in both languages. An independently generated fixture checks the encoder, and the comparison runner checks journal hashes and query results. Buffered writes belong in a separate comparison from synchronized writes because their acknowledgement contracts differ. The harness does not collect process CPU, RSS, allocation profiles, or physical device I/O. Its read-byte counters include data served from the page cache, and its table-size counter covers only logical entry payload. A sustained experiment needs those additional measurements and must run long enough for a slow worker to reach its lag limit. A short run with writes followed by catch-up cannot establish a service-level latency or freshness guarantee. Measure recovery to the serving state each policy actually requires. A journal-only service need not build a projection before answering queries. A projection-backed service may choose to finish replay before serving or expose partial progress. Recovering from a partial trailing record also needs testing separately from broader power-loss behavior.

sections.heading: What the local runs showed
sections.text: The measurements below were run locally on this machine: Component Configuration Processor Apple M3 Max, 16 CPU cores, arm64 (Mac15,9) Memory 128 GiB Operating system macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83 Storage Internal storage, APFS filesystem Toolchains Go 1.27.3 and Rust 1.99.1, optimized builds Runtime settings AC power; GOMAXPROCS=16; no CPU affinity or quota Runs used normal filesystem caching, without cache eviction or exclusive machine access. Each condition ran seven times in randomized order, with one benchmark process at a time. All 168 measured runs agreed on journal bytes and query results within their workloads; twelve warmup runs were excluded. These results describe this machine and workload, rather than a hardware-independent performance expectation. For the synchronized baseline, 100,000 records in batches of 64 took roughly seven seconds under each policy. The background worker showed no consistent acknowledgement advantage, and every synchronized background run peaked at just one batch of lag. Synchronization made this a poor workload for testing pressure on a 4,096-record budget. The longer buffered runs made the maintenance cost easier to see. Each wrote two million records across 4,096 possible keys. The table held only 64 KiB of logical entry data. These are medians of seven runs; the p99 columns summarize the seven per-run batch percentiles. Policy Go write + drain, ms Rust write + drain, ms Go batch ack p99, µs Rust batch ack p99, µs Journal only 124.95 116.19 12.46 12.21 Eager table 122.62 111.68 12.38 11.96 Background table 171.70 157.94 14.58 14.38 Figure 5: Seven runs per policy; diamonds mark medians. M3 Max, 16 cores, 128 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2, APFS. Vertical offsets separate overlapping points and have no data meaning. Buffered writes only; queries and recovery are outside the timed phase. Open the full-size plot Here, the background median elapsed time was about 40% higher than eager maintenance in both implementations. Its batch-acknowledgement p99 was higher too. Updating this small table directly was cheap; the worker added replay and coordination, including another logical read of all 64 MB of journal data. Moving that work into a worker did not pay off in this experiment. These buffered numbers do not describe synchronized-write throughput. Reducing both the lag limit and worker block to 64 records exercised tighter coordination. All fourteen background runs reached that bound without exceeding it. Median write-and-drain time rose to 206.73 ms in Go and 313.19 ms in Rust. Because both settings changed, and the unchanged eager controls also ran faster in this later campaign, I would not attribute an exact slowdown to the lag limit alone. The journal-only policy paid at query time: post-drain lookup p99 medians were about 28 ms in Go and 20 ms in Rust in the longer buffered workload, which included 36 absent-device queries out of 256. Table lookups were close to the timer's resolution. Those measurements show why the read workload matters; they do not predict HTTP latency or settle a language choice. A larger or more expensive projection could change the maintenance comparison, but this experiment has not demonstrated that benefit.

sections.heading: Choose the language at the constraint that matters
sections.text: For an existing Go ingestion service with adequate memory headroom and contained ownership boundaries, Go is a reasonable starting point. For a new storage component dominated by buffer recycling, reclamation, and shared mutable state, Rust's static ownership constraints can be a substantial advantage. Profiling should precede a rewrite. If synchronization accounts for an assumed 90% of operation time and stays unchanged, halving everything else reduces total time by 5%, equivalent to about a 1.053× speedup. That arithmetic does not predict either language's result. The Go worker runs in a goroutine; the Rust worker uses a dedicated standard-library thread. They have different scheduling models. These examples do not compare async runtimes. Both programs stop and join their worker on normal completion and returned errors. Go defers the stop-and-wait procedure before file cleanup. Rust performs it explicitly before propagating the write result; dropping a join handle alone would detach the thread. The full Rust worker also catches unwinding panics and explicitly publishes failure to wake waiters. That does not make shutdown generally panic-safe: the excerpts still panic on a poisoned mutex, and an abort or permanently blocked I/O operation lies outside that mechanism. Poisoning itself is advisory and does not establish whether the state is intact., For the operator refreshing the dashboard, the useful response is a value with a stated progress position, or a clear timeout waiting for the requested write. For the service, that promise has a cost: once replay falls far enough behind, new writes must wait or be rejected. I would establish that behavior under a mixed workload before using acknowledgement latency to choose an indexing policy or a language. The companion contains both journal implementations, an independent byte fixture, tests, and a comparison runner. The separate handoff examples illustrate buffer ownership; they are not another journal policy. Article excerpts omit setup and instrumentation and are not standalone programs. Checks passed with the project's pinned Go 1.27.3 and Rust 1.99.1 toolchains on macOS/arm64: nine core Go tests and two handoff tests with the race detector, vet for both Go packages, five core Rust tests and three handoff tests in debug and release, and the ownership compile-fail doctest in both profiles. Optimized binaries completed 168 measured runs with matching journal hashes and query checksums within each workload. Every measured background run stayed within its lag limit. The measurements use one writer, fixed-size records, a small dense table, and queries only after catch-up. They are local comparisons, not a production capacity estimate or a general performance ranking of Go and Rust. Concurrent live freshness, process-resource use, physical device I/O, and power-loss behavior remain unqualified.
